messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Heat maps are all the rage, so I want to do one
parts:
Hi Zach,

Welcome to the black-hole-vortex that is R! If I understand you correctly, these are your vairables:

1. inflamation marker
2. microbe genus
3. microbe abundance
4. time

It's hard to accurately show more than three variables in a single plot, but I could imagine you presenting three plots, one for each time point, with your inflamation markers on one axis, microbe identity on the other axis, and microbe abundance as a color. You can actually do this relatively easily with ggplot2 and the "tile" geom. This blog post shows it quite elegantly: https://martinsbioblogg.wordpress.com/2013/03/21/using-r-correlation-heatmap-with-ggplot2/

messages.author: 6e4e37c602c2b104
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Heat maps are all the rage, so I want to do one
parts:
Hi Zach,

Welcome to D-RUG!

How to visualize really depends on what point you’re trying to illustrate with the data. You can map variables to at least x, y, color, and size of points and then facet over a fifth variable. Point shape is another possibility, but it’s not as visually obvious as the others. One naive idea that comes to mind for your data is a separate pairs plot for each time point in your dataset, something like this:

d = data.frame(
    marker1 = rnorm(300),
    marker2 = rnorm(300),
    marker3 = rnorm(300),
    time = rep(1:3, each = 100)
)
dsplit = split(d, d$time)
lapply(dsplit, function(df) pairs(df[, -4], main = paste('time', unique(df$time))))

You could also color points by time point instead of faceting over that variable. But again, the right approach will depend on what conclusions you want to illustrate, as well as the size of your dataset and other factors. One other thought is that if you are really interested in the correlations and not the values, it might make sense to extract the correlation between each pair of markers and visualize those, e.g. using the corrplot function from the package of the same name.

We’d love to see you at the meetings, but note that they are Tuesdays this quarter: 3 - 5 in Wickson 2124. Cheers,

Michael

​

-- 
Michael Levy

messages.author: 6e4e37c602c2b104
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Heat maps are all the rage, so I want to do one
parts:
Hi Zach,

There is quite a lot of missingness in this data. You can tell cor() how to handle missingness with the use argument (see the “details” section of ?cor), but even having it scrape out every comparison it can make, there are some variables in your dataset that don’t share any observations, so you cannot calculate a correlation between them. cor returns NA for those, and corrplot won’t deal with NAs… that’s what produces the error you saw. To make it work, you could remove the columns with the worst missingness and/or have cor calculate correlations based on just where two variables both have an entry:

sum(complete.cases(d))
(missingness = sapply(d, function(x) sum(is.na(x))) / nrow(d))
d = d[, missingness < .5]
dcor = cor(d, use = 'pairwise.complete.obs')
library(corrplot)
corrplot(dcor)
​

-- 
Michael Levy

Hi Zach,

Welcome to D-RUG!

How to visualize really depends on what point you’re trying to illustrate with the data. You can map variables to at least x, y, color, and size of points and then facet over a fifth variable. Point shape is another possibility, but it’s not as visually obvious as the others. One naive idea that comes to mind for your data is a separate pairs plot for each time point in your dataset, something like this:

d = data.frame(
    marker1 = rnorm(300),
    marker2 = rnorm(300),
    marker3 = rnorm(300),
    time = rep(1:3, each = 100)
)
dsplit = split(d, d$time)
lapply(dsplit, function(df) pairs(df[, -4], main = paste('time', unique(df$time))))

You could also color points by time point instead of faceting over that variable. But again, the right approach will depend on what conclusions you want to illustrate, as well as the size of your dataset and other factors. One other thought is that if you are really interested in the correlations and not the values, it might make sense to extract the correlation between each pair of markers and visualize those, e.g. using the corrplot function from the package of the same name.

It's hard to accurately show more than three variables in a single plot, but I could imagine you presenting three plots, one for each time point, with your inflamation markers on one axis, microbe identity on the other axis, and microbe abundance as a color.
